unit.title: Apply principles and practices in electrical installation

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is electric current?
options: The push that drives electricity around a circuit
The force that stops electricity flowing
The flow of electrons around a circuit
The heat given off by a conductor

questions.stem: What does the voltage do in a circuit?
options: It pushes the current around the circuit
It slows the current down in the circuit
It stores the current until it is needed
It turns the current into light and heat

questions.stem: In a circuit, the resistance goes up and the voltage stays the same. What happens to the current?
options: The current goes up
The current doubles
The current stays the same
The current goes down

questions.stem: A 220 V water heater has a resistance of 11 Ω. What current does it draw?
options: 2 A

questions.stem: A 1100 W microwave oven is used on a 110 V circuit. What current does it draw?
options: 1 A

questions.stem: Two lamps are connected in series. What happens if one lamp fails?
options: The other lamp gets brighter
The other lamp stays the same
The breaker trips at once
Both lamps go out

questions.stem: Why are the lamps and socket outlets in a house wired in parallel?
options: Each gets full voltage and works on its own
So that they all switch on and off together
So that the total current is always smaller
So that one fault turns every one of them off

questions.stem: What does a kilowatt-hour (kWh) measure?
options: The voltage at the meter
The current in the service cable
The energy used, for the bill
The resistance of the heater

questions.stem: What is the usual supply voltage for lights and general socket outlets in a Jamaican home?
Which of these appliances in a Jamaican home is most likely to need a 220 V supply?
options: A bedside table lamp
A small phone charger
An electric stove
A portable radio

questions.stem: Why is copper the most common metal for conductors?
options: It is the cheapest metal you can buy anywhere
It conducts well and bends without breaking
It never gets warm when current flows
It is lighter than any other metal

questions.stem: Which of these is a good insulator?
options: Copper
Aluminium
Steel
PVC

questions.stem: What is the main reason for choosing a larger conductor size for a circuit?
options: To make the cable easier to bend into boxes
To make the circuit look neater
To lower the total price of the whole job
To carry more current without overheating

questions.stem: In the AWG system of wire sizes, which statement is true?
options: A larger number means a thicker wire
A smaller number means a thicker wire
The number is the length in metres
The number shows the voltage rating

questions.stem: Why does a cable have an outer sheath as well as insulation on each conductor?
options: To make the cable heavier so it lies flat
To show the size of the conductors inside
To protect the insulated cores from damage
To let the cable carry a higher voltage

questions.stem: In a lighting circuit, which conductor must the switch be connected in?
options: The line (live) conductor
The neutral conductor
The earth conductor
Any one of the conductors

questions.stem: Why must the switch be in the line conductor and not in the neutral?
options: So that the lamp uses less power when it is on
So the lamp holder is dead when the switch is off
So that the switch lasts longer before wearing out
So that the lamp lights more brightly

questions.stem: Which switching lets you control one lamp from two places, such as the top and the bottom of the stairs?
options: Two-way (three-way) switching
Single one-way switching
Dimmer and timer switching
Double-pole isolator switching

questions.stem: In two-way switching, what are the conductors that link the two switches called?
options: Neutral loops or returns
Earth links or bonds
Strappers or travellers
Supply tails (feeds)

questions.stem: Which switch is fitted between two two-way switches so that a lamp can be controlled from three places?
options: A one-way switch
A dimmer switch
A double-pole safety switch
An intermediate switch

questions.stem: In a lamp holder with a screw base, which part should the switched line conductor go to?
options: The outer screw shell
The earth terminal
The centre contact
The cord grip

questions.stem: Why should each socket outlet have an earth connection?
options: So that plugs fit more tightly into it
So the outlet uses less power each month
So the outlet stays cool when it is used
So earthed appliances are safe in a fault

questions.stem: Where is RCD (GFCI) protection most needed for socket outlets?
options: In bedrooms, living rooms and offices
In kitchens, bathrooms and outdoors
In hallways and on landings
In dry, locked store rooms

questions.stem: Why should a heavy appliance, such as a large air conditioner, have its own circuit?
options: So it does not overload a shared circuit
So it can be switched on from two places
So it can run on a different frequency
So that it needs no breaker to protect it

questions.stem: How should the rating of a circuit breaker compare with the cable it protects?
options: No more than the cable can safely carry
Twice what the cable can safely carry
Any size, as long as it fits the panel
Larger, so that it will never trip off

questions.stem: What is a short circuit?
options: A cable that has been cut too short to reach its terminal
Line touching neutral, so a very large current flows
A circuit that only feeds one or two outlets
A circuit that switches off after a short time

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the earth electrode at a building?
options: To bring the power company's supply into the building
To make the meter read correctly
To keep the voltage at 220 V
To connect the installation's earth to the ground

questions.stem: Why are metal water pipes bonded to the main earthing terminal?
options: To stop the water in them getting hot
To stop the pipes rusting in the ground
So they cannot become live in a fault
So the water heater uses less power

questions.stem: What do fuses and circuit breakers mainly protect against?
options: Low voltage coming from the supply
Lightning strikes on the roof or mast
Leaks of water into boxes
Overload and short-circuit currents

questions.stem: Why is PVC conduit widely used in Jamaican houses built of concrete block?
options: It conducts, so it can be used as the earth
It is heavier than steel, so it stays in place
It does not rust and can be set into walls
It needs no fixings, boxes or fittings at all

questions.stem: Why should a conduit not be filled with too many cables?
options: The conduit becomes too heavy to fix to the wall
Cables can overheat and be damaged pulling in
The cables will then carry far too little current
The conduit will soften and change its colour

questions.stem: Where must all joints in cables be made?
options: In a box or enclosure that can be reached later
Inside the wall, covered over with plaster
In the middle of a long conduit run, taped up
Anywhere, as long as they are wrapped in tape

questions.stem: What is a cable gland or bush used for where a cable enters a box?
options: To join two cables together inside the box
To protect the cable and hold it firmly
To earth the box to the cable
To make the box waterproof only

questions.stem: How should cables be run on the surface of a wall?
options: Diagonally, taking the shortest route
Loosely, so that they can move freely
In curves, so that they look decorative
Straight and level or plumb, fixed evenly

questions.stem: Which type of outlet box should be used outdoors?
options: A weatherproof type, with its seal in place
An indoor type, painted over with house paint
Any type, as long as it is fixed high up
An open type, so that rain can drain out

questions.stem: What does an electrical layout drawing (plan) of a house show?
options: The colour of the walls in every room
The price of each material for the job
Where the outlets, switches and lights go
The names of the family who will live there

questions.stem: Why do electricians use standard symbols on drawings?
options: To make the drawing look more modern and neat
So the drawing can be printed in colour
So everyone reads the drawing the same way
So that no words or notes are ever needed

questions.stem: On a drawing, what does the scale 1:50 mean?
options: 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on the building
1 mm on the drawing is 50 metres on the building
The drawing is in 50 separate parts
There are 50 outlets in the whole building

questions.stem: When a conductor is fitted into a terminal, how much bare copper should show outside the terminal?
options: About 10 mm, so it is easy to test it
About 5 mm, so that it can cool down
Enough to wrap twice around the screw
None: insulation should go right up to it

questions.stem: Why must terminal screws be tight?
options: So the cover will fit back onto the box
A loose joint can get hot and start a fire
So the conductor can be pulled out easily
So the breaker will trip less often later

questions.stem: Why are conductors identified (marked) at both ends?
options: So each one can be traced and connected right
So the cable looks brighter and more colourful
So the conductor can carry a larger current
So the installation costs less to put in

questions.stem: Before a new installation is switched on for the first time, what must be done?
options: Switch on all the lights to see if any are dead
Inspect it and carry out the dead tests
Wait one week for the plaster to dry
Ask the customer to plug in every appliance

questions.stem: Which of these tests is done with the installation dead?
options: Testing the RCD with an RCD tester
Checking that the lights work
Insulation resistance test
Measuring the supply voltage

questions.stem: After all the dead tests on a practice board have passed, who connects it to a supply at the Centre?
options: Any trainee who finished their part first
The customer, on their own, at home
A visitor to the workshop
The instructor, after checking it

questions.stem: Before you start to change a light fitting in a house, what must you do?
options: Switch off at the wall switch, then begin
Take out the lamp, then work quickly
Wear rubber gloves and work on it live
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove it dead

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the law that says the current equals the voltage divided by the resistance?
Two 20 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is their total resistance, in ohms?
What is the name of the device that switches off a circuit when too much current flows, and can then be reset?
What is the name of the board or panel that holds the circuit breakers for all the circuits in a house?
What is the name of the tube, often made of PVC, that cables are run inside in walls and ceilings?
What two letters name the kind of current supplied by the mains, which changes direction many times each second?
What do we call the part of a circuit, such as a lamp or a heater, that uses the electrical energy?
What three letters name the plastic most often used to insulate cables and to make conduit?
How many watts are there in 1 kilowatt?
What is the name of the plastic cap with a spring inside that is twisted onto conductor ends to join them in a box?
What is the name of the switching where one switch controls a lamp from one place only?
What do we call the drawing that uses symbols to show how the parts of a circuit are connected, but not where they are in the building?
In a 110 V single-phase circuit, what is the name of the conductor that carries the current back to the supply?
What is the name of the electrical quantity that opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms?
What is the name of the test that checks that each switch is in the line conductor and that lamp holders and outlets are connected the right way round?

essays.stem: Explain Ohm's law and the power formula, and use them to work out the current and resistance of a 2200 W heater on a 220 V supply.
essays.modelAnswer: Ohm's law tells us how voltage, current and resistance are linked. The current (I) equals the voltage (V) divided by the resistance (R): I = V ÷ R. It can also be written V = I × R or R = V ÷ I. The power formula says that power (P), in watts, equals the voltage times the current: P = V × I, so I = P ÷ V. For a 2200 W heater on a 220 V supply, the current is I = P ÷ V = 2200 ÷ 220 = 10 A. The resistance of the heater element is R = V ÷ I = 220 ÷ 10 = 22 Ω. Knowing the current helps the electrician choose a cable and a circuit breaker that can carry 10 A safely, with the breaker rating not above what the cable can carry. If the same heater were wrongly run on 110 V, it would draw only half the current and give only a quarter of the heat.
markingPoints: States Ohm's law correctly (I = V ÷ R, or its other forms)
States the power formula P = V × I
Calculates the current correctly: 2200 ÷ 220 = 10 A
Calculates the resistance correctly: 220 ÷ 10 = 22 Ω
Links the current to choosing a suitable cable and breaker

essays.stem: Compare series and parallel circuits, and explain why the lamps and socket outlets in a house are wired in parallel.
essays.modelAnswer: In a series circuit the parts are connected one after another, so there is only one path for the current. The same current flows through every part, and the supply voltage is shared between them. The total resistance is all the resistances added together. If one lamp fails, the path is broken and every lamp goes out. In a parallel circuit each part is connected across the supply on its own branch. Every branch gets the full supply voltage, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents. If one lamp fails, the others keep working. The total resistance is less than the smallest branch. House lamps and outlets are wired in parallel so that each one gets the full 110 V or 220 V it is made for, each can be switched on and off by itself, and a fault in one does not stop the others. The circuit breaker must be sized for the total current of all the branches.
markingPoints: Series: one path, same current through each part, voltage shared
Series: total resistance is the sum; one failure stops all
Parallel: each branch gets the full voltage; currents add up
Parallel: one failure does not stop the others; total resistance is less than the smallest branch
Explains why houses use parallel: full voltage, separate control, faults do not stop other loads

essays.stem: Describe how a one-way lighting circuit is connected, and explain the safety reasons for the way it is wired.
essays.modelAnswer: A one-way lighting circuit lets one switch control one or more lamps from one place. The supply comes from a breaker in the distribution board. The line conductor goes to one terminal of the switch, and from the other switch terminal a switched line conductor goes to the lamp holder's centre contact. The neutral goes straight to the lamp holder's outer screw shell. The earth conductor goes to the earth terminal of the switch box, the light fitting and any metal parts. The switch is put in the line conductor so that when it is off, the lamp holder is dead and a person changing a lamp is not exposed to the supply. The line goes to the centre contact so that the outer shell, which is easy to touch, is connected to neutral. The earth makes sure a fault on a metal fitting trips the breaker. Before any work, the circuit is isolated, locked off and proved dead.
markingPoints: Line to the switch; switched line from the switch to the lamp
Neutral straight to the lamp holder
Earth to every box, fitting and metal part
Switch in the line so the lamp holder is dead when switched off; line to the centre contact
States that work is done only after isolation and proving dead

essays.stem: Explain what two-way switching is, where it is used, and how it works.
essays.modelAnswer: Two-way switching lets one lamp, or a group of lamps, be switched on or off from two different places. In some places the switches are called three-way switches. It is used where people need to control a light from each end, such as at the top and bottom of stairs, at both ends of a long passage, or at two doors of a large room. Each two-way switch has a common terminal and two other terminals. The line conductor goes to the common terminal of the first switch. Two conductors, called strappers or travellers, link the two other terminals of the first switch to the two other terminals of the second switch. The common terminal of the second switch feeds the switched line to the lamp, and the neutral goes to the lamp. Moving either switch changes which strapper carries the current, so the lamp can be turned on or off from either place.
markingPoints: Explains that one lamp is controlled from two places
Gives a suitable use, such as stairs or a long passage
Line to the common of the first switch; common of the second switch to the lamp
Two strappers (travellers) link the other terminals of the two switches
Explains that either switch changes the path, so it can turn the lamp on or off

essays.stem: Explain the purpose of earthing and bonding in an electrical installation.
essays.modelAnswer: Earthing connects the exposed metal parts of an installation, such as metal boxes, light fittings and the cases of appliances, to the general mass of the earth through protective conductors, the main earthing terminal and an earth electrode. If a line conductor touches a metal part, the fault current flows through the earth path back to the supply. This large current makes the breaker or fuse operate quickly, so the metal does not stay live and nobody gets a shock. Bonding joins other metal parts that are not part of the electrical system, such as metal water pipes, gas pipes and steel frames, to the main earthing terminal. This keeps all the metal at the same voltage, so a person who touches two metal parts at the same time does not get a shock between them. Earthing also gives RCDs (GFCIs) a path to detect a leak. All earth and bonding connections must be tight and must not be removed.
markingPoints: Earthing connects exposed metal parts to earth through protective conductors and the earth electrode
Fault current flows through the earth path and makes the protective device operate quickly
Stops metal parts staying live, protecting people from shock
Bonding joins pipes and other metal parts so they stay at the same voltage
Connections must be sound and never removed (or RCDs rely on the earth path)

essays.stem: Explain how an electrician chooses the cable and the circuit breaker for a new circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: First the electrician works out how much current the circuit will carry by adding up the loads, using I = P ÷ V. For example, a 220 V circuit for appliances of 3300 W in total would carry about 15 A. Next a cable is chosen whose current rating, from the maker's tables, is more than that current, allowing for how the cable is installed, such as in conduit, in a hot roof space, or bunched with other cables, because these make it run hotter. A long run may need a larger cable so the voltage drop is not too great. Then a circuit breaker is chosen whose rating is equal to or more than the circuit current but not more than the current the cable can safely carry. This way the breaker trips before the cable can overheat. The electrician follows the maker's tables, the drawing and the Centre's rules, and checks with the supervisor.
markingPoints: Works out the circuit current from the load (I = P ÷ V)
Chooses a cable whose rating is above the circuit current, from the maker's tables
Allows for installation conditions (conduit, heat, bunching) and voltage drop on long runs
Breaker rating at least the circuit current but not more than the cable rating
Explains that the breaker must trip before the cable overheats

essays.stem: Describe good workmanship when installing PVC conduit, boxes and accessories.
essays.modelAnswer: Good workmanship starts with following the drawing and marking out the positions of boxes and conduit runs with a tape measure and spirit level. Conduit is run straight, level or plumb, never at odd angles, so that hidden runs can be found later. Conduit is cut square and deburred so the cables are not damaged, and bends are made smoothly with a bending spring, with no kinks. Joints are made with the right fittings and solvent cement, and the conduit is fixed with saddles at even spacing as the maker says. Boxes are fixed firmly, level and flush with the finished wall. The conduit is not overfilled, so the cables can be drawn in without damage. All joints in conductors are made inside boxes that can be reached later. Conductors are left long enough to terminate neatly, with no bare copper showing. At the end, accessories are fitted straight, waste is cleared and the work is checked.
markingPoints: Follows the drawing and marks out accurately
Runs conduit straight, level or plumb, cut square, deburred and bent without kinks
Uses proper fittings and fixes conduit with saddles at even spacing
Fixes boxes firmly and level; does not overfill conduit; makes joints only in accessible boxes
Terminates neatly, fits accessories straight, cleans up and checks the work

essays.stem: Describe the inspection and dead tests that are done before a new installation is switched on, and explain why they are done before switching on.
essays.modelAnswer: Before a new installation is connected to the supply, it is inspected and tested dead. The inspection is a careful look at the work: the right cables and breakers are fitted, connections are tight, there is no bare copper showing, boxes and covers are fitted, conductors are identified, and the work matches the drawing. Then the dead tests are carried out with the supply off and locked off. The continuity of the earth (protective) conductors is tested, to be sure every metal part is earthed. The insulation resistance between conductors and to earth is tested, to be sure there are no faults that could cause a shock or fire. Polarity is checked, so that switches are in the line conductor and outlets are connected correctly. These tests are done before switching on because a wrong connection or an earth fault could cause a shock, a fire or an explosion the moment power is applied. Only after they pass does the instructor or supervisor switch on.
markingPoints: Visual inspection: correct parts, tight terminations, covers on, matches the drawing
Continuity of protective (earth) conductors
Insulation resistance between conductors and to earth
Polarity: switches in the line, outlets correct
Explains that faults found dead prevent shock or fire at switch-on; supervisor switches on after passing

essays.stem: Explain how an electrician reads an electrical layout drawing and uses it to plan an installation.
essays.modelAnswer: A layout drawing is a plan of the building that shows where the electrical points go. First I read the title block to check the job, the drawing number and the date, so I know it is the latest copy. I read the legend, which explains each symbol, such as a socket outlet, a switch, a light point and the distribution board. I note the scale, for example 1:50, so that I can measure distances on the drawing and work out the real lengths of conduit and cable. I count each kind of symbol to make a list of the boxes, accessories and fittings needed. I follow the lines that show which switch controls which light and which points are on each circuit. From this I write a materials list and plan the order of work. If anything on the drawing is unclear or does not match the building, I ask my supervisor before starting.
markingPoints: Checks the title block for the job, drawing number and date
Uses the legend to understand the symbols
Uses the scale to work out real lengths of cable and conduit
Counts the symbols to make a materials list and plans the order of work
Asks the supervisor if anything is unclear or does not match

essays.stem: Explain the dangers of poor terminations, and describe how to make a good termination at a screw terminal.
essays.modelAnswer: A termination is where a conductor is connected to a terminal. A poor termination can be loose, have strands cut off, have bare copper showing, or have insulation trapped under the screw. A loose or poor joint has a high resistance, so it gets hot when current flows. It can burn the accessory, melt the insulation and start a fire. Bare copper outside the terminal can be touched or can touch another conductor, causing a shock or a short circuit. To make a good termination, I first make sure the circuit is isolated and proved dead. I strip only enough insulation for the terminal, using wire strippers set to the right size so the copper is not nicked. For a screw terminal I form a loop clockwise, the way the screw tightens, or push a straight end fully into a pillar terminal. I tighten the screw firmly, check that no bare copper shows, and give the conductor a gentle pull to make sure it is held.
markingPoints: Describes poor terminations: loose, damaged strands, bare copper or trapped insulation
Explains that a loose joint overheats and can cause fire
Explains that exposed copper can cause shock or short circuit
Strips the right length without nicking, after isolation
Loops clockwise or inserts fully, tightens firmly, no bare copper, and does a pull test

practical1.title: Wire a one-way lighting circuit and a socket outlet on a practice board, then test it dead
practical1.brief: As a group, wire a small installation on the Centre's practice board from the circuit diagram the assessor gives: one one-way switch controlling a lamp holder, and one socket outlet, both fed from a terminal block that stands for the breaker in the distribution board. The board is NOT connected to any supply while you work. Use the conductor colours set by the Centre's rules, and connect the earth conductor to every box, fitting and earth terminal. Share the work so that every member wires and terminates part of it while another member checks it against the diagram: (1) read the diagram and list the materials, (2) fix the boxes and run the cables or conduit, (3) terminate the switch and lamp holder, with the switch in the line and the line to the lamp holder's centre contact, (4) terminate the socket outlet and the earth connections, (5) carry out the dead tests: continuity of the earth conductors, insulation resistance, and polarity, and record them. In a group of 4, one member does two stages; every member makes at least two terminations. Only when every dead test has passed does the instructor connect the board to the Centre's protected test supply and switch on, with the group standing clear. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the test record once for the whole group.
materials: Practice board with mounting space, not connected to any supply
A one-way switch, a lamp holder and lamp, a socket outlet, boxes and a terminal block
Cable or PVC conduit with single-core conductors, saddles or clips, and fixings
Electrician's hand tools: screwdrivers, wire strippers, side cutters, pliers, tape measure, spirit level
A low-resistance ohmmeter or multimeter and an insulation resistance tester
Safety glasses and safety boots for every member
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The circuit diagram and the materials list, with the materials laid out
The boxes fixed and the cables or conduit run neatly, straight and level
The switch terminations, with the switch in the line conductor
The lamp holder and socket outlet terminations, with every earth connected
A dead test being carried out, with the meter display in view
The finished board, with covers fitted, before the instructor's switch-on
checklist: Read the circuit diagram correctly and helped list the materials
Fixed boxes and ran cables or conduit straight, level and secure
Stripped conductors to the right length without nicking the copper
Put the switch in the line conductor and the line to the lamp holder's centre contact
Connected the earth conductor to every box, fitting and earth terminal
Made tight terminations with no bare copper showing outside the terminals
Carried out and recorded a dead test correctly
Stood clear and did not touch the board while the instructor switched it on
Cleaned up the work area and returned the tools
safety: The board must not be connected to any supply while you work; only the instructor connects it, after the dead tests pass
Never touch the board while it is connected; the instructor switches off and isolates it before any change
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping, and keep fingers clear of blades
Keep the floor clear of off-cuts; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Draw and wire a two-way lighting circuit on a practice board, and test it dead
practical2.brief: As a group, draw and then wire a two-way lighting circuit, so that one lamp can be switched on and off from two places, such as the top and bottom of a staircase. The practice board is NOT connected to any supply while you work. Stage 1 (about 45 minutes): together, draw a neat circuit diagram on the sheet given, showing the supply, the two two-way switches with their common terminals, the two strappers (travellers), the lamp and the earth conductor, and a short materials list. The assessor checks the diagram before you start wiring. Stage 2: share the wiring so that every member terminates at least one switch or the lamp while another member checks it against the diagram, using the conductor colours set by the Centre's rules and marking the strappers clearly. Stage 3: carry out the dead tests (earth continuity, insulation resistance, and a continuity check that the lamp circuit is made in every switch position) and record them. Each member explains to the assessor how two-way switching works. Only when every dead test has passed does the instructor connect the board to the Centre's protected test supply and try each switch, with the group standing clear. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the diagram and test record once for the whole group.
materials: Practice board, not connected to any supply
Two two-way switches with boxes, a lamp holder and lamp, and a terminal block for the supply
Cable or PVC conduit with single-core conductors, markers for the strappers, and fixings
A multimeter or low-resistance ohmmeter and an insulation resistance tester
Safety glasses and safety boots for every member
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The finished circuit diagram and materials list, signed off by the assessor
The boxes and cable or conduit runs fixed on the board
The first two-way switch terminated, with the common and strappers marked
The second two-way switch and the lamp holder terminated
A continuity check in one switch position, with the meter display in view
The finished board with covers fitted, before the instructor's switch-on
checklist: Helped draw a correct circuit diagram with the common terminals and strappers shown
Followed the diagram when wiring and checked another member's work against it
Connected the line to the common of the first switch and the lamp to the common of the second
Marked the strappers clearly and terminated them tightly
Connected the earth conductor to every box and fitting
Carried out and recorded a dead test correctly
Explained clearly how two-way switching lets either switch turn the lamp on or off
Stood clear while the instructor switched the board on, and left the area tidy
safety: The board must not be connected to any supply while you work; only the instructor connects it, after the dead tests pass
Never touch the board while it is connected
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping
Keep tools and off-cuts off the floor; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
